title: Public Influence
blurb: Ways that people, orders, and fashions hold sway.

words.definition: An expression of opinion or the ability to be heard.
words.note: A voice can mean participation, not just sound: having a voice in a decision means having a say.
words.origin: Anglo-Norman voiz, from Old French vois
hints: Used when discussing participation.
Having one matters even when nobody is speaking aloud.
words.connection: A voice lets a person contribute to public debate.

words.definition: Influence or power to affect a decision.
words.note: Clout can also mean a blow. In discussions of influence, it refers to practical power rather than an official title.
hints: Often discussed in negotiations.
Some people can get a decision changed without holding an official post.
words.connection: Clout is the influence that makes other people listen.

words.definition: An authoritative order.
words.note: An edict announces a decision from an authority. It leaves less room for negotiation than a request.
words.origin: Latin edictum, from Old French edit
hints: Belongs to the language of authority.
The speaker expects obedience rather than discussion.
words.connection: An edict is an exercise of public authority.

words.definition: The prevailing fashion or popularity of something.
words.note: The phrase in vogue describes what is currently favoured; its opposite is out of fashion.
words.origin: Middle French vogue, from Old Saxon wogōn
words.example: Miniskirts were the vogue in the '60s.
hints: Often used of tastes that change.
What is admired this season may be forgotten next year.
words.connection: Vogue describes the influence of a prevailing fashion.

words.definition: The period during which a ruler holds power.
words.note: Reign also works as a verb. Rain concerns weather; rein concerns restraint.
words.example: The reign of Victoria was a long one.
hints: Can describe an era as well as a person's actions.
A successor brings this period to an end.
words.connection: A reign is the period during which a ruler holds power.

title: No Clear Answer
blurb: Five ways a conversation can withhold clarity.

words.definition: To avoid or escape something, often deliberately.
words.note: Evading a question is different from misunderstanding it: the avoidance is the action.
words.origin: Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō
words.example: He evaded his opponent's blows.
hints: Often used when accountability is at stake.
A question may receive many words and still go unanswered.
words.connection: To evade a question is to avoid answering it.

words.definition: To qualify a statement or limit a risk.
words.note: In speech, words such as perhaps and usually can soften a claim. In finance, a hedge limits exposure to risk.
words.example: Diversify your financial portfolio to hedge price risks.
hints: Can describe an uneasy commitment.
A promise qualified by several conditions might do this.
words.connection: Hedging makes an answer less definite.

words.definition: Understood without being said.
words.note: From the Latin tacere, to be silent — the same root as taciturn. A tacit agreement is binding precisely because nobody wrote it down.
words.origin: Middle French tacite, from Latin tacitus
words.example: There must have been a tacit understanding between them.
hints: Concerns how understanding is communicated.
Two people may agree without ever discussing the matter.
words.connection: A tacit understanding remains unspoken.

words.definition: Not clearly expressed or defined.
words.note: A vague instruction leaves details uncertain. An ambiguous one may support two distinct meanings.
words.origin: Middle French vague, from Latin vagus
words.example: Their descriptions of human behavior become vague, dull, and unclear.
hints: Often appears in criticism of instructions.
The reader is left asking exactly what was meant.
words.connection: A vague reply withholds a clear meaning.

words.definition: To vanish rather than have the conversation.
words.note: In conversation, ghost is an informal verb for abruptly ending contact without explanation. The figurative disappearance is the useful link to its older noun sense.
hints: Has uses beyond stories told in the dark.
An unanswered conversation can acquire a permanent silence.
words.connection: To ghost someone is to stop responding entirely.

title: Shades of Feeling
blurb: Five distinct kinds of emotional experience.

words.definition: Fear of something not here yet.
words.note: The useful distinction: fear points at something present, dread points at the future. Dread is the more exhausting of the two.
words.example: The dread presence of the headmaster.
hints: Often concerns an event still ahead.
Waiting for the news may be worse than receiving it.
words.connection: Dread is an uneasy feeling about what is coming.

words.definition: A small doubt that arrives uninvited.
words.note: Originally meant a sudden wave of sickness or faintness. The modern sense kept the physical suddenness and moved it into the conscience.
words.origin: Old English cwealm, from German quellen; in English since the 16th century
hints: Often interrupts a decision.
A small moral hesitation can survive a confident argument.
words.connection: A qualm is a moment of doubt or unease.

words.definition: Burning enthusiasm, usually for a person.
words.note: From the Latin ardere, to burn — the same root as arson. English kept the heat and dropped the damage.
words.example: They were imbued with a revolutionary ardor.
hints: Can describe a person's commitment.
A cause can inspire the same intensity as a romance.
words.connection: Ardor is a feeling of passionate enthusiasm.

words.definition: Dread with no particular object.
words.note: Taken whole from German, via Freud and Kierkegaard. English had no word for anxiety-about-nothing-specific, which is a strange gap for English to have had.
words.origin: German Angst, from Old High German angust
hints: Appears in discussions of identity.
The uncertainty may concern one's whole life rather than tomorrow's appointment.
words.connection: Angst is a deep and often unfocused anxiety.

words.definition: Warm, laughing happiness.
words.note: Shares a root with merry. It is specifically the sociable kind of joy — you can be happy alone, but mirth wants company.
words.example: This joke is a source of mirth for the audience.
hints: Usually belongs to a shared occasion.
Laughter at the table can be a sign of it.
words.connection: Mirth is the pleasure expressed in amusement and laughter.

title: Money Moves
blurb: Resources can be held, accumulated, contributed, or dishonestly acquired.

words.definition: Anything you own that counts for something.
words.note: From the Anglo-French aver assetz, to have enough. The singular asset was reverse-engineered from assets, which came first.
words.origin: Anglo-Norman asetz, from Old French assez
words.example: Assets have earning power or some other value to their owner.
hints: Used when assessing a position.
A useful skill can count just as much as something owned.
words.connection: An asset is a resource with value.

words.definition: A long con dressed as a business.
words.note: American carnival slang from around 1900. It implies patience — a grift is worked, not pulled.
hints: Often appears around an apparently attractive offer.
The profit depends on somebody believing a dishonest story.
words.connection: Grift acquires money through deception.

words.definition: A tenth, given whether you want to or not.
words.note: A tithe traditionally names a tenth of income or produce given to a church. It is more specific than a general donation.
words.origin: Old English tēoþa, from Old English tēoþian
hints: Associated with an established obligation.
Traditionally, a portion of a harvest could fulfil it.
words.connection: A tithe is a contribution of one tenth, traditionally to a church.

words.definition: To accumulate well past the point of use.
words.note: Not the same as a horde, which is a crowd. One is treasure, the other is people, and they are unrelated words that sound identical.
hints: May be motivated by uncertainty.
The owner accumulates things but is reluctant to use them.
words.connection: To hoard is to accumulate and retain resources.

words.definition: Payment for a decision.
words.note: Originally a piece of bread given to a beggar. It drifted from charity to theft to corruption in about three hundred years.
hints: A transaction someone would rather keep quiet.
The payment is meant to change another person's official decision.
words.connection: A bribe purchases improper influence.

title: An Open Book
blurb: The language of books, from their description to their physical pages.

words.definition: A short puff of praise on a cover.
words.note: Invented in 1907 by humorist Gelett Burgess, who put a fictional Miss Belinda Blurb on a book jacket as a joke. The joke became the industry standard.
hints: Often encountered before deciding what to read.
It has very little space in which to make a book sound inviting.
words.connection: A blurb is the short description that presents a book.

words.definition: A leaf of a book or manuscript.
words.note: A leaf has two sides. Manuscript references can identify a leaf and then specify its recto or verso.
words.origin: Medieval Latin foliō, from Latin folium
hints: Belongs to the vocabulary of books and manuscripts.
An archivist might use this unit when locating a passage in an old manuscript.
words.connection: A folio is a leaf of a manuscript or book.

words.definition: The front of a leaf, usually the right-hand page.
words.note: Recto and verso distinguish the two sides of a leaf. On an ordinary open book, the recto is on the right.
hints: Used when planning the layout of a book.
An illustrator may reserve this side for the opening image of a chapter.
words.connection: Recto names the front of a leaf, usually the right-hand page.

words.definition: The reverse of a leaf, usually the left-hand page.
words.note: Verso is paired with recto in descriptions of books, manuscripts, and prints.
hints: Used by people describing printed objects.
A printer might inspect this side for ink showing through from the other.
words.connection: Verso names the reverse of a leaf, usually the left-hand page.

words.definition: Written or spoken language without metrical verse structure.
words.note: Prose can still have rhythm. What distinguishes it from verse is its form, not a lack of musicality.
words.origin: Old French prose, from Latin prōsa
words.example: Though known mostly for her prose, she also produced a small body of excellent poems.
hints: Describes how language is arranged.
A novel and a report usually share this form.
words.connection: Prose is ordinary written language rather than verse.

title: Fall and Rise
blurb: A sequence of changing fortunes: decline, low point, recovery, ascent, and peak.

words.definition: A marked decline in activity, value, or performance.
words.note: A slump can describe a posture, an economy, or a spell of poor form.
hints: Can apply to performance or posture.
A difficult season can leave figures well below their earlier level.
words.connection: A slump is a decline in fortunes or activity.

words.definition: The lowest possible point.
words.note: From the Arabic nazir, opposite — it is the astronomical point directly beneath you, exactly opposite the zenith. Arabic gave English most of its star vocabulary.
words.origin: Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت
hints: Often used when describing changing fortunes.
Think of the turning point before a recovery.
words.connection: The nadir is the lowest point of the fall.

words.definition: To recover strength or confidence after a setback.
words.note: The verb can also mean gathering people for a shared purpose. Both uses suggest renewed strength.
words.example: The market fell this morning but rallied later in the day.
hints: Often follows a discouraging period.
A weakened team or market can find renewed strength.
words.connection: To rally is to recover after a decline.

words.definition: A sudden strong increase or forward movement.
words.note: A surge can be physical, emotional, or numerical: water, hope, and demand can all surge.
words.origin: Middle French sourgir, from Latin surgō
words.example: Stimulated a surge of speculation.
hints: Describes a change with momentum.
A graph might suddenly become much steeper.
words.connection: A surge is a strong upward movement in this account of changing fortunes.

words.definition: The highest part of a wave, ridge, or rise.
words.note: At the crest of a wave can describe a moment of great success as well as a physical position.
words.origin: Old French creste, from Latin crista
hints: Can describe a stage of success.
After the ascent comes a moment with nothing higher immediately ahead.
words.connection: The crest is the high point of the rise.

title: After Affection
blurb: Images and actions from a love affair and its aftermath.

words.definition: What is still warm after the fire.
words.note: An unusually old word, barely changed from Old English aemerge. It has always meant the part that outlasts the thing itself.
hints: Often appears after a more dramatic event.
Something apparently finished may still hold a little heat.
words.connection: An ember provides a metaphor for affection that survives a relationship.

words.definition: A meeting arranged in secret.
words.note: Originally a hunting term: the appointed place where you waited for the game to be driven towards you. Make of that what you will.
words.origin: Old French triste, from Old Norse treysta
hints: Associated with secrecy and anticipation.
Two people have arranged to meet away from other eyes.
words.connection: A tryst is a private meeting between lovers.

words.definition: To reject with contempt.
words.note: Originally meant to kick. The physical sense survives in the word's tone — to be spurned is worse than to be refused.
words.example: She spurned his advances.
hints: Describes a deliberate response to an offer.
The refusal carries more contempt than a simple no.
words.connection: To spurn is to reject affection with disdain.

words.definition: To feel a loss openly.
words.note: Related to memory through an old root meaning to be anxious or remember. Mourning is etymologically an act of remembering, not of sadness.
hints: Can concern something that cannot return.
The loss need not be a person's death.
words.connection: Mourning can follow the loss of a relationship.

words.definition: To want something distant, continuously.
words.note: Shares a root with the German gern, gladly. The ache and the gladness are the same word underneath, which feels about right.
hints: Often involves distance or absence.
Wanting something becomes an ache rather than a passing thought.
words.connection: Yearning is the longing left by an absent lover.

title: Physical Effort
blurb: The body’s energy, strength, and work.

words.definition: The point of the exercise.
words.note: One of the oldest words in English, cognate with the Sanskrit svedas. Humans have needed this word for as long as there have been words.
hints: Can be a visible consequence of effort.
A demanding climb may leave it on a collar.
words.connection: Sweat is a bodily response to physical effort.

words.definition: A tendon; also, muscular strength.
words.note: Sinews connect muscles to bones. Figuratively, the word suggests the resources that give something strength.
hints: Used both anatomically and figuratively.
A writer may use it to suggest the underlying strength of a body or organisation.
words.connection: Sinew transmits the force produced by muscles.

words.definition: Physical force and liveliness.
words.note: From the Latin vigere, to be lively — the same root as vigil and vigilant. Staying awake and being strong were once the same idea.
hints: Describes the manner in which something is pursued.
A person can return from rest with renewed reserves of it.
words.connection: Vigor is the energy brought to an effort.

words.definition: Physical, especially muscular, strength.
words.note: Brawn is often paired with brains when contrasting strength and intelligence.
words.example: The builders at the site had more brawn than brain.
hints: Often contrasted with another kind of ability.
The task needs lifting power rather than a clever argument.
words.connection: Brawn is muscular strength.

words.definition: To apply force, influence, or effort.
words.note: One exerts pressure on something, or exerts oneself in doing something demanding.
words.example: He considered exerting his influence on John to gain an advantage for himself.
hints: Usually needs an object after it.
Pressure, influence, or effort can all follow this verb.
words.connection: To exert oneself is to make a physical effort.

title: Words of Reproach
blurb: Five labels that criticise a person’s character.

words.definition: A likeable scoundrel; or something gone off-script.
words.note: Appeared suddenly in the 1560s with no clear ancestor. A word for people who go off on their own that itself came from nowhere.
hints: Can describe a person who disregards expectations.
Charm may soften the judgement, but the rules still go unfollowed.
words.connection: Rogue is a reproach for an unprincipled person.

words.definition: A dishonest man of low standing.
words.note: Originally just meant boy, with no insult intended. It spent five hundred years sliding downhill, which is the usual fate of words for young men.
hints: Often encountered in older stories.
A character so described is not to be trusted with the purse.
words.connection: Knave is an old insult for a dishonest man.

words.definition: Someone rude by disposition.
words.note: Meant a free peasant — a social rank, not a judgement. Churlish is what the upper classes decided that rank implied.
words.origin: West Midland Middle English churle, from Old English ċeorl
hints: A judgement about someone's conduct.
Hospitality is unlikely from a person described this way.
words.connection: Churl reproaches a person for being rude and mean-spirited.

words.definition: Someone excessively concerned with propriety.
words.note: This is a judgemental label, not a neutral description of a person with boundaries.
hints: Appears in disputes about propriety.
Someone finds even mildly improper behaviour unacceptable.
words.connection: Prude criticises an excessively prudish person.

words.definition: A person who hoards money and is reluctant to spend it.
words.note: A miser may possess plenty. The defining trait is unwillingness to part with money, not poverty.
words.example: Scrooge was a typical miser: spending nothing he could save, nor enjoying his wealth.
hints: A character defined by an attitude to possessions.
Having enough does not make this person willing to spend.
words.connection: Miser reproaches someone who hoards money and avoids spending it.

title: Running on Empty
blurb: Resources and enthusiasm worn down towards exhaustion.

words.definition: Used up, with nothing held back.
words.note: The same word for money and for energy, which is not a metaphor English chose so much as one it never questioned.
hints: Describes a condition after use.
There may be nothing left to draw on.
words.connection: Spent describes exhausted reserves.

words.definition: Wearied or dulled by overexposure.
words.note: Being jaded suggests that repetition has worn away interest, even in something once enjoyable.
words.example: The amoral, jaded, bored upper classes.
hints: Can follow too much of an initially pleasing thing.
Another fine meal or grand promise no longer impresses.
words.connection: Jaded describes enthusiasm worn away by overexposure.

words.definition: What is left at the bottom.
words.note: From Old Norse dregg. One of the many words Vikings left in English, alongside sky, knife, and — fittingly — ransack.
words.example: The dregs of society should be taken to the garbage dump.
hints: Often considered only at the end.
The last pour may contain what everyone else left behind.
words.connection: Dregs are the remnants left after the desirable part is used.

words.definition: Unsteady and slightly unreal.
words.note: Origin genuinely unknown — it simply appears in American English in the 1890s. Possibly a blend of woozle and boozy, possibly nothing.
words.example: Sami looked woozy because he had been drinking.
hints: Concerns how someone feels rather than what they think.
Standing up quickly might make the room seem unreliable.
words.connection: Wooziness can accompany physical exhaustion.

words.definition: Tired in body or patience.
words.note: Weary of something means tired of it. Wary of something means cautious about it.
hints: Often follows a prolonged demand.
Rest may be wanted, or simply an end to the repetition.
words.connection: Weary describes tiredness of body or patience.

title: At the Counter
blurb: Actions and ingredients used in preparing food.

words.definition: To work dough with your hands.
words.note: An Old English word, and a close relative of the German kneten. Unrelated to need, which is a much older and gloomier word that merely sounds the same.
hints: An action whose effects build through repetition.
Hands work a mixture until its texture changes.
words.connection: Kneading develops dough before baking.

words.definition: To spoon the fat back over.
words.note: Confusingly, there is an unrelated baste meaning to sew loosely, and a third meaning to beat soundly. English kept all three and let context sort it out.
hints: Usually happens more than once during preparation.
A cook returns liquid to the surface as heat does its work.
words.connection: Basting moistens food during cooking.

words.definition: A leaf you were told to like.
words.note: Short for Swiss chard, which is not Swiss. A Swiss botanist named it, and the label stuck to a Mediterranean plant that had never been near the Alps.
words.origin: Middle French carde, from Latin carduus
hints: Encountered among ingredients.
A cook might give its stalks longer in the pan than its leaves.
words.connection: Chard is a leafy vegetable used in cooking.

words.definition: To beat air into something.
words.note: The tool is named after the action, not the other way round. The verb comes from an Old Norse word for a rapid sweeping movement, which is also why a train can whisk you somewhere.
hints: The action and the implement share a name.
Air can enter a mixture through rapid movement.
words.connection: Whisking mixes ingredients during preparation.

words.definition: The fungus doing all the work.
words.note: The root means to boil or foam, which is what people could actually observe. Nobody knew yeast was alive until Pasteur, but the word had described its behaviour for a thousand years.
hints: A small ingredient with a large effect over time.
Warmth and patience can matter as much as the amount added.
words.connection: Yeast makes dough rise through fermentation.

title: Cold Outside
blurb: Conditions and descriptions of cold weather.

words.definition: Ice formed straight out of the air.
words.note: Shares a root with freeze, obviously, but also with the word for a hard crust. Frost is etymologically the skin the cold puts on things.
hints: Often noticed early in the morning.
An exposed surface can acquire a delicate white covering.
words.connection: Frost forms when water vapour deposits as ice.

words.definition: The worst of both.
words.note: A Germanic word with cousins across northern Europe, which is roughly the distribution of people who have needed a specific word for this.
hints: Can make a journey unpleasant.
What falls is less soft than snow and less liquid than rain.
words.connection: Sleet is wintry precipitation involving ice or mixed rain and snow.

words.definition: An unpleasant coldness.
words.note: Chill can name a cold sensation or describe cooling something. A chill in a conversation is figurative.
words.example: There was a chill in the air.
hints: Can describe a sensation or an atmosphere.
A draft can bring it into an otherwise comfortable room.
words.connection: A chill is a sensation of cold.

words.definition: Cold in a way you are supposed to enjoy.
words.note: Probably a reshaping of the French brusque. The same word gave English both brisk and brusque, which now describe a pleasant walk and an unpleasant person.
hints: Can describe both movement and surroundings.
A walk may feel lively because the air is sharp.
words.connection: Brisk air is invigoratingly cool.

words.definition: Covered with or characterised by snow.
words.note: Snowy can describe weather, a landscape, or something resembling the colour of snow.
words.example: A long snowy winter.
hints: Describes the appearance of a place.
A landscape may lose its familiar colours beneath a white covering.
words.connection: Snowy describes a landscape or day marked by snow.

title: The Heist
blurb: False documents, suspects, and a planned robbery.

words.definition: To make. To fake.
words.note: The same word for honest smithing and dishonest documents, both from the Latin fabricare, to fashion. The forger and the blacksmith are doing etymologically identical work.
hints: Can describe a productive or a dishonest act.
A signature can be made by someone who has no right to make it.
words.connection: To forge documents is to create false evidence for a crime.

words.definition: Proof you were somewhere else.
words.note: Latin for elsewhere, and originally used in English exactly that literally. It only came to mean the excuse itself, rather than the fact, in the twentieth century.
hints: Usually concerns a disputed event.
A claim about being elsewhere can change an investigation.
words.connection: An alibi places a suspect somewhere other than the crime scene.

words.definition: Someone convicted of a serious crime.
words.note: Also, still, a medical term for an infection at the fingertip. The two senses have coexisted for centuries with no one much bothered by it.
words.origin: Old French felon, from Early Medieval Latin fellōnem
hints: A legal description of a person.
It implies a serious conviction rather than mere suspicion.
words.connection: A felon has been convicted of a serious crime.

words.definition: A crime with a sense of humour.
words.note: From the Italian capriola, a goat's leap — the same root as Capricorn. A caper is named for skipping about, which is why the word refuses to sound serious.
hints: Can be mischievous or criminal.
In a film, an elaborate plan may be described this way.
words.connection: A caper can be an adventurous criminal undertaking.

words.definition: A robbery with a plan.
words.note: American underworld slang from the 1920s, almost certainly a pronunciation of hoist. To hoist goods was to steal them long before anyone pulled a heist.
hints: Often implies planning and accomplices.
A valuable target and an escape route belong in the same story.
words.connection: A heist is a planned robbery tying the criminal vocabulary together.

title: Between Waking
blurb: Experiences and actions around sleep and wakefulness.

words.definition: What you would rather be doing.
words.note: The Old English dream meant joy, music, or revelry — not sleep at all. The modern sense probably arrived from Old Norse and quietly replaced it.
hints: Can refer to an experience or an ambition.
Its events need not obey the rules of the waking day.
words.connection: Dreams can occur during sleep.

words.definition: Deliberate wakefulness.
words.note: From the Latin vigilia, a watch kept at night — the same root as vigour and vigilant. Staying awake, being strong and paying attention were once one idea.
words.origin: Old French vigile, from Latin vigilia
hints: Often sustained for a reason.
A bedside chair or a candle can accompany the long hours.
words.connection: A vigil is a period deliberately spent awake.

words.definition: To bring someone round.
words.note: Began as a falconry term for a hawk shaking its feathers. It moved from birds to people to crowds, gathering force at every step.
hints: Describes a change in someone's state.
A call or sudden noise may do it.
words.connection: To rouse someone is to wake them.

words.definition: The period of darkness between sunset and sunrise.
words.note: Night can be a time of rest or activity. The word names the period, not what happens during it.
hints: A familiar division of time.
Artificial light can make this period less noticeable indoors.
words.connection: Night is the usual period for sleep.

words.definition: The reason you are awake.
words.note: One of a family of words English built straight from the sound: snore, snort, sneeze, snarl, sniff. The initial sn- doing the work of a nose.
hints: Often noticed by somebody else.
The person responsible may deny having made any sound.
words.connection: Snoring is a sound made during sleep.

title: Making Music
blurb: Words, delivery, harmony, and pace in music.

words.definition: The bit before the chorus.
words.note: From the Latin versus, a turning — specifically the turn of a plough at the end of a furrow. A line of poetry is named after where the writing turns back.
words.origin: Old English fers, from Latin versus
hints: A division as well as a form.
A song may return to a refrain after one of these.
words.connection: A verse supplies a section of a song's words.

words.definition: A song for a funeral.
words.note: From dirige, the first word of a Latin antiphon sung in the office for the dead. An entire genre named after the opening word of one hymn.
hints: Associated with a solemn occasion.
The audience is more likely to be grieving than dancing.
words.connection: A dirge is music of mourning.

words.definition: To sing low and close to the microphone.
words.note: A Scots and northern English word for a low murmur, which was sitting unused until amplification made quiet singing possible in the 1920s.
words.origin: Scots croon, from Middle Dutch crônen
hints: Describes a manner of performance.
The delivery is intimate and gentle rather than projected across a hall.
words.connection: To croon is to sing softly.

words.definition: Notes agreeing to be heard together.
words.note: Shortened from accord, meaning agreement. The spelling with an h was borrowed later from cord, the string — so the word has two unrelated ancestors fused together.
hints: Its elements are heard together.
Several pitches can form one harmonic event.
words.connection: A chord combines notes in music.

words.definition: How fast the thing goes.
words.note: Italian for time, straight from the Latin tempus. Most of the vocabulary of Western music is Italian because Italy was where the notation was standardised.
hints: Concerns the unfolding of an activity.
A conductor can change it without changing the written pitches.
words.connection: Tempo determines music's pace.

title: Too Little
blurb: The language of limited money and resources.

words.definition: To squeeze. To economise. To steal.
words.note: All three senses are the same word narrowing and widening over six hundred years. Feeling the pinch and pinching something are cousins.
hints: Can describe a difficulty without literal contact.
An unexpected bill can put someone in one.
words.connection: A pinch is a period of financial difficulty.

words.definition: Barely enough.
words.note: From Old Norse skamt, short. It is one of the few English adjectives that still sounds slightly wrong as a verb, though scanting was once perfectly ordinary.
words.origin: Old Norse skamt, from Middle English scanten
hints: Often precedes a resource or amount.
There is something available, but barely enough.
words.connection: Scant resources provide little to live on.

words.definition: To use or provide too little.
words.note: Skimping on preparation may save time at first and cost more later.
hints: Describes a choice about resources.
Quality may suffer when too little is allowed for the task.
words.connection: To skimp is to spend or use too little.

words.definition: Plain, minimal, or more than is needed.
words.note: Spare has contrasting uses: a spare style has little extra, while a spare key is an extra one.
hints: Can describe a room, a style, or an amount.
The absence of anything extra is the useful idea.
words.connection: Spare describes something kept to a minimum.

words.definition: The same thing, said sadly.
words.note: Originally the past participle of break, used of a merchant whose business had broken. Bankrupt is the same idea in Italian: banca rotta, a broken bench.
hints: Often temporary, but inconvenient.
An invitation may need to wait until payday.
words.connection: Broke means having no money available.

title: An Attachment
blurb: The language of romantic interest and pursuit.

words.definition: A feeling with no plan attached.
words.note: The romantic sense is American, from the 1880s, and the metaphor is physical: being crushed. English chose the most violent available verb for the least dangerous feeling.
hints: Can be felt long before it is declared.
An ordinary encounter becomes disproportionately exciting.
words.connection: A crush is an early romantic attraction.

words.definition: A love affair, especially in literary usage.
words.note: Borrowed from French, amour keeps a literary tone in English. It is not the ordinary everyday word for love.
words.origin: Middle French amour, from Latin amor
words.example: L'amour, it causes many fatalities, does it not?
hints: More common in literary writing than casual speech.
A discreet affair might be described with this borrowed word.
words.connection: An amour is a love affair.

words.definition: To go weak in a satisfying way.
words.note: An Old English word meaning to faint, related to a root for suffocating. It survived mostly because Victorian novelists found it so useful.
hints: Often used with deliberate exaggeration.
Admiration can be described as almost overwhelming the body.
words.connection: To swoon can express an overwhelming romantic response.

words.definition: To pursue, patiently and visibly.
words.note: The same word as a royal court, and that is the point: courting meant behaving as one did at court, with all its formality and audience.
words.origin: Old French cort, from Latin cohors
hints: A verb as well as several familiar nouns.
Attention is offered in the hope of winning affection.
words.connection: To court is to seek a romantic relationship.

words.definition: To signal interest deniably.
words.note: First meant to flick or dart something away — you could flirt a fan open. The human sense came from the quick, glancing movement.
hints: Often leaves room for uncertainty.
The interest may be sincere, playful, or both.
words.connection: Flirting communicates possible romantic interest.

title: At the Office
blurb: Identity, targets, responsibilities, retention, and changes of strategy.

words.definition: What a company believes it is.
words.note: Originally a burning piece of wood, then the mark burned into livestock to show ownership. Every brand is etymologically a scar proving who owns the animal.
hints: Can identify something without naming its maker.
Reputation and a recognisable identity both matter.
words.connection: A brand gives a business its public identity.

words.definition: A number someone else chose.
words.note: From the Latin quota pars, how great a part. It entered English as accounting vocabulary and has been used to apply pressure ever since.
words.origin: Latin quota pars, from Latin quota
words.example: All the salesmen met their quota for the month.
hints: Belongs to the language of allocation.
A manager may discuss it before a month of work and measure it afterwards.
words.connection: A quota sets a business target.

words.definition: An assigned area of responsibility.
words.note: A project can fall within or outside a team’s remit. As a verb, remit has other uses, including sending payment.
hints: Describes the extent of responsibility.
A task outside it may properly belong to somebody else.
words.connection: A remit defines a person's area of work.

words.definition: Customers leaving as fast as they arrive.
words.note: From the butter churn: violent repetitive motion that produces a result. Business borrowed the agitation and quietly dropped the part where you get butter.
words.origin: Old English ċyrn, from Old English ċernan
hints: Can describe movement or repeated loss.
A company may measure how often customers leave.
words.connection: Customer churn is a measure of business retention.

words.definition: Admitting the plan was wrong, expensively.
words.note: A pivot is the fixed pin a thing turns on — so a company that pivots is claiming, flatteringly, that it has not moved at all.
hints: Can be physical or strategic.
A fixed point remains while the direction changes.
words.connection: A business pivot changes strategic direction.

title: Look Up
blurb: Bodies, motion, and shadows in the sky.

words.definition: A sudden violent brightening.
words.note: Origin unknown, appearing in the 1500s meaning to spread outward. The light sense and the trouser sense are the same word doing the same job.
hints: Often brief and conspicuous.
A quiet surface can suddenly release a burst of light.
words.connection: A solar flare is a burst of energy from the Sun.

words.definition: The fully shaded inner region of a shadow.
words.note: The umbra contrasts with the penumbra, where the light source is only partly obscured.
hints: Used when describing changes in light.
An observer within this region has a different view of an eclipse.
words.connection: The umbra is the darkest part of an eclipse shadow.

words.definition: Of the moon.
words.note: The same root gives lunatic, from a genuine old belief that the moon's phases affected the mind. The medical term outlived the theory by centuries.
words.origin: Latin lūnāris, from Middle French lunaire
hints: Describes an association.
A calendar can follow this cycle instead of the Sun's.
words.connection: Lunar phenomena concern the Moon.

words.definition: A path that keeps falling and missing.
words.note: From the Latin orbita, a wheel track or rut. It also still means the bony socket of your eye, which is the older English sense.
hints: Can describe influence as well as motion.
A smaller body remains tied to a larger one while moving around it.
words.connection: An orbit is the path of a body around another in space.

words.definition: Ice on a very long loop.
words.note: From the Greek for long-haired — komētēs. The Greeks named it for the tail, describing it as a star wearing its hair loose.
words.origin: Old English comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης
words.example: Halley's comet has been known about since prehistoric times.
hints: A visitor that may be expected again.
Near the Sun it can develop a striking visible trail.
words.connection: A comet is an icy body travelling around the Sun.

title: Seeing Red
blurb: Anger, provocation, and the malice they can produce.

words.definition: Wanting worse for someone, at your own cost.
words.note: A shortening of despite, which meant contempt. In spite of still carries the original sense: doing something in contempt of an obstacle.
words.origin: Old French despit, from Latin dēspiciō
words.example: He was so filled with spite for his ex-wife, his brother was afraid of what he might do.
hints: Can motivate a small, deliberate act.
Hurting someone may matter more than gaining anything.
words.connection: Spite is ill will expressed through a wish to hurt.

words.definition: Angry, and slightly formal about it.
words.note: From the Latin ira, anger — the same root as ire and irascible. It is the word newspapers use when they mean furious but want to sound neutral.
words.example: How would you deal with an angry or irate customer?
hints: Describes a person's state.
A sharply worded complaint might come from someone like this.
words.connection: Irate means very angry.

words.definition: Anger with the volume of a sermon.
words.note: Built from an Old English word meaning twisted or bent — the same root as writhe and wreath. Rage as something that contorts you.
hints: Often found in elevated or dramatic language.
A warning may concern the consequences of provoking it.
words.connection: Wrath is intense anger.

words.definition: Wound up, usually on purpose.
words.note: An American variant of roiled, meaning to stir up sediment in water. To rile someone is to make them cloudy.
hints: Describes the result of provocation.
A needling remark has had its intended effect.
words.connection: Riled describes someone made angry.

words.definition: Poison, or the tone of voice.
words.note: From the Latin venenum, which originally meant a potion or drug of any kind — including love potions, and shares a root with Venus.
words.origin: Old French venim, from Classical Latin venēnum
hints: Has a figurative use in speech.
The words can wound even though nothing physical is injected.
words.connection: Venom describes the malice in bitter speech.

title: False Appearances
blurb: Ways to disguise an intention or misdirect another person.

words.definition: Confidence standing in for cards.
words.note: Also a steep headland, and the two are unrelated. The poker sense came from a Dutch word meaning to brag; the cliff is a separate nautical borrowing.
hints: Often depends on another person's uncertainty.
Confidence is displayed despite an unconvincing position.
words.connection: A bluff misrepresents the strength of one's position.

words.definition: To perform a feeling you do not have.
words.note: From the Latin fingere, to shape or mould — the same root as fiction and figment. Pretending and sculpting were once the same verb.
words.origin: Old French feindre, from Latin fingere
hints: A verb concerning appearances.
The emotion on display may not be felt at all.
words.connection: To feign is to pretend a feeling or condition.

words.definition: The version you are presenting.
words.note: From the same Germanic root as wise, as in likewise and in no wise — meaning manner or way. A guise is literally a way of appearing.
words.example: He hides his true feelings under the guise of indifference.
hints: Concerns how someone or something is presented.
A harmless appearance can conceal a different purpose.
words.connection: A guise is an outward appearance that can disguise intent.

words.definition: To cover something deliberately.
words.note: The garment is named after its shape: the Medieval Latin clocca meant a bell, and a hanging cloak looks like one. Clock comes from the same word.
words.origin: Old Northern French cloque, from Medieval Latin clocca
hints: A familiar object can also supply a verb.
An intention may be hidden as effectively as a body.
words.connection: To cloak something is to conceal it.

words.definition: Something used to lure attention away from a real target.
words.note: A decoy works by being noticed. Concealment and deception do not always require invisibility.
hints: Works by attracting attention.
The real target benefits when attention goes elsewhere.
words.connection: A decoy deceives by drawing attention to a substitute.

title: Recorded Sound
blurb: The formats, containers, and divisions of physical recordings.

words.definition: The format that refused to die.
words.note: Coined by chemists from the Latin vinum, wine, because the compound was first derived from ethanol. The word for records is named after wine.
hints: Both a material and a shorthand for a format.
A collection might be played with a needle.
words.connection: Vinyl records store sound in physical grooves.

words.definition: A cylinder around which thread, film, or tape is wound.
words.note: Spool is also a computing verb: work can be queued for later processing, as with a print job.
words.origin: Old Northern French spole, from Middle Dutch spoele
hints: Used to manage a long flexible material.
Winding and unwinding are central to its purpose.
words.connection: A spool holds the tape used in older recording media.

words.definition: Recorded, transmitted, or reproduced sound.
words.note: Audio can stand alone as a noun or describe another noun, as in audio recording.
words.example: I DMed him an audio of myself singing the South Park intro.
hints: Refers to one part of a recording.
It remains when the picture is switched off.
words.connection: Audio is the sound preserved by recording media.

words.definition: An individual recording or a recorded channel.
words.note: A track may be a complete song, while a multitrack recording combines separately recorded parts.
words.origin: Old French trac, from Old Norse traðk
hints: Can divide a larger recorded work.
Listeners might skip ahead to a favourite one.
words.connection: A track is a section of a recording.

words.definition: Cylinders or frames on which film or tape is wound.
words.note: A reel holds a length of material so it can be wound and unwound. Film and tape gave the word lasting associations with recording.
hints: Objects associated with winding.
A projectionist once had to change these during a film.
words.connection: Reels hold the film or tape used for recordings.

title: Beyond the Road
blurb: Features of a wooded rural landscape.

words.definition: A stream. Also, to tolerate.
words.note: Two unrelated words. To brook no argument comes from an Old English verb meaning to use or enjoy, which has nothing to do with water.
hints: Often encountered away from buildings.
It can be crossed without the engineering a river demands.
words.connection: A brook is a small stream in a rural landscape.

words.definition: Open scrubby ground.
words.note: Heathen comes from it: a heath-dweller, someone living out past the settlements where the new religion had not reached. An insult built out of a landscape.
hints: Describes a kind of open land.
Low shrubs thrive where a forest does not dominate.
words.connection: A heath is open shrub-covered countryside.

words.definition: A clearing with light in it.
words.note: Probably related to glad, which originally meant bright or shining rather than happy. A glade is the bright patch in a dark wood.
words.example: I yearned for the glades of the New Forest or the shingle of Southsea.
hints: An interruption within a landscape.
Sunlight reaches a space surrounded by trees.
words.connection: A glade is an open space in a wood.

words.definition: The white one.
words.note: Among the oldest tree names in the language, traceable to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning bright — named for the bark, thousands of years ago.
hints: Recognised as much by its surface as its shape.
Pale peeling bark can make it stand out among neighbours.
words.connection: Birch is a tree found in woodland.

words.definition: A small deliberate wood.
words.note: An Old English word with no known relatives in other languages — unusual for such a common word. It has meant the same thing for as long as English has existed.
hints: Describes a grouping.
Several trees can form one without making a whole forest.
words.connection: A grove is a small group of trees.

title: Raise a Glass
blurb: Drinks, the words that accompany them, and the absence of intoxication.

words.definition: Raising a glass to someone.
words.note: Genuinely from toasted bread: spiced toast was dropped into wine to flavour it, and the person honoured was said to be the toast of the drink.
hints: Can accompany a shared occasion.
A few words may precede raised glasses.
words.connection: A toast is spoken while raising a drink.

words.definition: Beer brewed with yeast that works at low temperatures.
words.note: Lager is a broad family of beers, not a guarantee of one colour or strength.
hints: Usually encountered in a glass.
Patience at cool temperatures matters in its production.
words.connection: Lager is a family of beers.

words.definition: Dark, and a meal in itself.
words.note: The beer is named after the adjective meaning strong or thickset. Stout ale simply meant strong ale, and the noun outlived the phrase.
words.example: Stout is darker, stronger and sweeter than porter beer.
hints: A description of build also names a drink.
In a glass, a dark colour and roasted flavour are likely.
words.connection: Stout is a dark style of beer.

words.definition: Deceptively strong.
words.note: Traces back through Latin and Greek to a Hebrew word, shekar, meaning strong drink. It arrived in English via the Bible before it meant apples specifically.
words.origin: Old French cisdre, from Hebrew שֵׁכָר
words.example: Which do you like better? Apple cider, or champagne?
hints: A seasonal harvest provides its starting point.
An orchard can supply the contents of a glass.
words.connection: Cider is made from apples.

words.definition: Tomorrow's problem, solved early.
words.note: From the Latin sobrius, which appears to be se- (without) plus ebrius (drunk) — the same ebrius behind inebriated. Sober is literally un-drunk.
words.origin: Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius
hints: Describes a condition or a manner.
The judgement concerns the absence of intoxication, not necessarily cheerfulness.
words.connection: Sober describes someone who is not intoxicated.

title: Something Moved
blurb: A sequence of stealth, unease, and fearful reactions.

words.definition: To move slowly and wrongly.
words.note: The noun for an unpleasant person is American, from the 1880s. The plural the creeps — that crawling sensation — is older than the insult.
hints: Often concerns movement that attracts little notice.
Speed is sacrificed to avoid being heard.
words.connection: Creeping is a stealthy movement that can create suspense.

words.definition: To shake without deciding to.
words.note: An Old English verb, and a Quaker was originally a mocking nickname — for people said to tremble at the word of the Lord. The group kept the insult.
words.example: I felt the ground quaking beneath my feet.
hints: A reaction can share its name with an event.
Fear may be visible in a person's unsteady body.
words.connection: To quake is to tremble with fear.

words.definition: To make yourself smaller.
words.note: From a Middle Low German word meaning to squat or crouch. Unrelated to coward, which comes from the Latin for tail, as in an animal turning tail.
hints: A response involving posture.
A threat can make someone shrink towards the ground.
words.connection: To cower is to crouch in fear.

words.definition: Wrong in a way you cannot name.
words.note: Originally Scots and northern English, and it first meant fearful rather than frightening — you were eerie, the ghost was not. The word swapped ends.
words.example: The eerie sounds seemed to come from the graveyard after midnight.
hints: Describes an atmosphere.
Nothing is visibly wrong, yet the silence feels unnatural.
words.connection: Eerie surroundings create a sense of unease.

words.definition: Fear that arrives all at once.
words.note: Named for the god Pan, who was believed to cause sudden groundless terror in lonely places. One of the few emotions named after a specific deity.
words.origin: Middle French panique, from Ancient Greek πανικός
hints: Can interrupt considered action.
An urgent fear leaves little room for a careful decision.
words.connection: Panic is sudden overwhelming fear.

title: At the Table
blurb: The risks, tokens, and chance outcomes of gambling.

words.definition: Nothing to do with skill.
words.note: Luck came into English from Dutch or Low German, and it arrived through gambling — the earliest English uses are all about games of chance.
hints: Often said after an outcome.
The result was favourable without necessarily being earned.
words.connection: A lucky outcome favours the player by chance.

words.definition: Money placed on an opinion.
words.note: From an Old North French word related to gage, a pledge — the same root as engage and mortgage. A wager was originally the security, not the bet.
hints: Involves something put at risk.
An opinion becomes more consequential when money backs it.
words.connection: A wager stakes value on an uncertain outcome.

words.definition: A win you cannot repeat.
words.note: From nineteenth-century billiards, for an accidentally successful shot. There are also fluke the flatfish and fluke the parasite, all three unrelated.
words.example: We've classified by a fluke; actually, the first goal was just a total fluke.
hints: Usually resists reliable repetition.
A success may tell us very little about the method.
words.connection: A fluke is an unlikely success attributed to chance.

words.definition: What you stand to lose.
words.note: Probably from the literal stake — a post driven into the ground, on which the prize was placed for all to see. The money sat on a stick in the middle.
hints: A reason to care about the outcome.
What is put forward may be lost if the prediction fails.
words.connection: A stake is what a gambler risks.

words.definition: Money, made easier to lose.
words.note: Casinos use tokens precisely because chips do not feel like money. The word is just the ordinary chip, a small fragment, doing psychological work.
hints: Small objects can represent a larger value.
At some tables, money is exchanged for these before play.
words.connection: Chips stand in for money at gaming tables.

title: Ways of Speaking
blurb: Five ways speech can be delivered or used.

words.definition: Someone else's words, borrowed.
words.note: From the Latin quotare, to number — medieval scribes quoted a text by marking it with numbers to reference it. The sense of repeating came later.
words.origin: Old French coter, from Latin quotus
hints: Concerns another person's words.
Accuracy matters when repeating them as evidence.
words.connection: To quote is to reproduce someone's words.

words.definition: To answer an argument properly.
words.note: From an Old French word meaning to thrust back, built on but, an end or blow — the same root as butt. A rebuttal is a headbutt with sources.
hints: An action in an exchange of arguments.
A claim is met with reasons it should not stand.
words.connection: To rebut is to answer an argument with opposing evidence.

words.definition: Speech taking its time.
words.note: Probably a frequentative of draw, as in drawing the words out. English builds a lot of verbs this way: sparkle from spark, crackle from crack.
hints: Concerns delivery rather than content.
The sounds seem to take their time leaving the speaker.
words.connection: A drawl is a slow, lengthened manner of speaking.

words.definition: Provocation dressed as a joke.
words.note: Possibly from the French tant pour tant, tit for tat — a taunt as a reply given in kind. Fittingly, the word for a comeback may itself be a comeback.
words.origin: Middle French tanter, from Old French tempter
hints: Speech with a particular intention.
The speaker wants discomfort or an angry reaction.
words.connection: To taunt is to provoke someone with words.

words.definition: Advertising yourself.
words.note: Origin uncertain, in English since the 1200s. It once meant a threat as much as a brag, which tells you something about how boasting was received.
hints: Often concerns the speaker's own achievements.
The listener may feel that admiration is being requested too insistently.
words.connection: To boast is to speak with excessive pride.

title: Cloth and Clothing
blurb: Fabrics and garments made from cloth.

words.definition: The most successful fabric ever made.
words.note: From serge de Nîmes, the French town. Jeans are named after Genoa by the same logic, so a pair of denim jeans is named after two cities at once.
hints: Often valued for durability.
Workwear helped make this material familiar.
words.connection: Denim is a woven cloth used in clothing.

words.definition: A durable twill fabric with diagonal ribs.
words.note: Serge has traditionally been used for suits and uniforms. Twill names the weave rather than one particular fibre.
words.origin: Old French sarge, from Old Chinese 絲
hints: A material with a distinctive weave.
Uniforms and suits are traditional uses for it.
words.connection: Serge is a twill fabric used for garments.

words.definition: A dress, said fondly.
words.note: Originally a monk's habit, which is why a disgraced priest is defrocked. The word travelled from monastery to wardrobe and kept only one foot in each.
hints: A word with an old-fashioned everyday feel.
An invitation might prompt someone to choose a new one.
words.connection: A frock is a dress.

words.definition: A blanket with better manners.
words.note: Arrived in English from Persian via Urdu, along with the garment itself, in the eighteenth century. One of many textile words English imported wholesale.
words.origin: Hindi शाल, from Classical Persian شال
hints: Worn without requiring fitted sleeves.
It can be draped when the evening becomes cool.
words.connection: A shawl is a piece of cloth worn around the shoulders.

words.definition: Cloth for pretending to like walking.
words.note: Almost certainly a misreading. A clerk wrote tweel — Scots for twill — and someone read it as tweed, thinking of the river. The error became the name.
words.origin: Scots tweedling, from Middle English twel
hints: Often associated with country clothing.
Its woollen surface can look flecked or subtly patterned.
words.connection: Tweed is a woollen fabric used in clothing.

title: Under the Skin
blurb: Body structures, a circulating fluid, and a sign of circulation.

words.definition: Proof of the obvious.
words.note: From the Latin pulsus, a beating — the same root as impulse and repel. There is also pulse the lentil, entirely unrelated, from a word for porridge.
words.origin: Anglo-Norman puls, from Old French pous
hints: Can be assessed without looking inside.
A fingertip at the wrist may detect it.
words.connection: A pulse is the rhythmic expansion of an artery.

words.definition: The other circulatory system.
words.note: From the Latin lympha, clear spring water — which was itself probably an alteration of nympha, the water spirit. A body fluid named after a nymph.
words.origin: French lymphe, from Ancient Greek νῠ́μφη
words.example: You have a cold and your lymph nodes are swollen.
hints: Discussed in relation to circulation and immunity.
Swelling can prompt a doctor to consider how this fluid is draining.
words.connection: Lymph is a fluid carried through the lymphatic system.

words.definition: The one doing the grinding.
words.note: From the Latin mola, a millstone. Named for the job rather than the shape, by people who ground their own flour and saw the resemblance daily.
hints: An everyday part of the body with a specialised job.
Its work becomes especially noticeable when chewing something tough.
words.connection: A molar is a grinding tooth.

words.definition: Wiring. Also, audacity.
words.note: The Latin nervus meant sinew or bowstring — the Greeks and Romans did not distinguish nerves from tendons. The confusion is preserved in the word.
words.origin: Medieval Latin nervus, from Latin nervus
hints: Can name a structure or a quality.
Messages travel through the body along it.
words.connection: A nerve carries signals between parts of the body.

words.definition: The structural argument.
words.note: The Latin spina meant a thorn. The backbone is named after its spiky projections, which is also why a hedgehog's spines and your spine are one word.
hints: An ordinary noun that also appears in publishing.
Damage here can affect support and movement throughout the body.
words.connection: The spine is the body's central column of vertebrae.

title: A Matter of Time
blurb: Measuring time, naming its periods, and being early or late.

words.definition: Time going missing.
words.note: From Old French delaier, built on the Latin dilatare, to spread out or widen. A delay is etymologically time being stretched rather than lost.
hints: Creates a difference between intention and arrival.
Something expected now must wait.
words.connection: A delay pushes an event later in time.

words.definition: A stretch of time with a character.
words.note: From a Greek word meaning a stopping point — the fixed moment from which time is measured, not the span itself. The modern sense inverts the original.
words.origin: Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή
hints: Used when discussing a broad sweep of history.
The interval is distinguished by a defining change or character.
words.connection: An epoch is a notable period of time.

words.definition: Late, officially.
words.note: From the Latin tardus, slow — the same root as retard in its original neutral sense of delay. It is the word institutions use when they mean late.
hints: A judgement relative to an expectation.
The arrival happens after it was due.
words.connection: Tardy describes lateness.

words.definition: Fast, and paying for it.
words.note: Haste arrived from Old French but goes back to a Germanic root meaning violence or force. Hurrying was originally an act of aggression.
hints: Concerns how an action was taken.
There may have been too little time for consideration.
words.connection: Hasty describes action taken with excessive speed.

words.definition: The thing you are losing to.
words.note: From the Medieval Latin clocca, a bell, because early public clocks marked hours by ringing rather than by a face. Cloak comes from the same word.
words.origin: Middle Dutch clocke, from Medieval Latin clocca
hints: An ordinary object with several specialised forms.
Its purpose is to make passing intervals legible.
words.connection: A clock measures and displays time.

title: Losing the Argument
blurb: Five ways a disagreement stops going your way in public.

words.definition: A reply that outperforms the post it answers.
words.note: In arithmetic this is simply a comparison of two quantities, and the online sense keeps that exactly: it weighs the response against the original. The verb form spread on Twitter around 2017.
hints: Arithmetic lent this one to the timeline.
A comparison of two numbers, used as a verdict.
words.connection: Being out-measured by the person answering you is the first sign the room has turned.

words.definition: An answer sent back to whoever spoke first.
words.note: From Old French replier, to fold back, from Latin replicare. The same root gives replicate and replica, all carrying the idea of folding something over on itself.
words.origin: Old French replier, from Latin replicō
hints: Folding something back on itself, originally.
What arrives underneath, often in numbers.
words.connection: Every public argument begins with someone answering.

words.definition: To cut someone off from reaching you.
words.note: The word began as a solid lump of wood, and the sense of obstruction came from putting such a lump in the way. The social media meaning is the newest branch of a very old tree.
words.origin: Old French bloc, from Middle Dutch blok
hints: Started life as a lump of timber.
An obstruction, now also a button.
words.connection: The last move available when answering has stopped working.

words.definition: Someone who provokes for the reaction alone.
words.note: Two separate words collided here. The Norse creature of folklore is unrelated to the fishing sense, dragging a baited line slowly through water, and it is the fishing one the internet meaning almost certainly comes from.
words.origin: Old Norse trǫll, from Danish trold; in English since the early 17th century
hints: Folklore and fishing both claim this word.
Dragging bait slowly and waiting.
words.connection: The provocation is the point, not the position.

words.definition: Public mockery, delivered for an audience.
words.note: From basketball, where the ball is pushed down through the hoop from above. Before that it meant to dip something into liquid, from a Middle High German word.
hints: Basketball gave this its modern swagger.
Before the court, it meant dipping something.
words.connection: Scoring off someone from above, where everyone can see it.

title: High Praise
blurb: Five ways to call something good without using the word.

words.definition: Admirably willing to hold an unpopular view.
words.note: Popularised by the rapper Lil B in the early 2010s, who took a word that had been an insult and turned it into praise for being yourself regardless of judgement. The approving sense grew outward from his following.
hints: One rapper turned an insult into a compliment.
Praise aimed at nerve, not at taste.
words.connection: Approval for conviction rather than for agreement.

words.definition: Said of music that lands with force.
words.note: The sense comes straight from the physical blow, something that arrives hard. It spread through Bay Area hip-hop, where the noun described a track with heavy bass.
hints: Bay Area bass culture carried this one.
A physical blow, repurposed as a review.
words.connection: Approval borrowed from the force of an impact.

words.definition: Describes a performance that wins completely.
words.note: The older sense is to kill, from Old English slean, to strike. The admiring use was carried into wider speech by Black and Latino ballroom culture.
hints: Ballroom culture lent this to everyone else.
Its old meaning was far more violent.
words.connection: Approval phrased as total victory over the room.

words.definition: Belonging to the best of a group.
words.note: From French elite, the chosen, from Latin eligere, to pick out. The same root gives elect and eligible.
words.origin: Old French elit, from Latin eligere
hints: Latin for picking out the chosen few.
Shares a root with elect and eligible.
words.connection: Approval that places something at the top of a field.

words.definition: Reasonable, and worth taking seriously.
words.note: From Latin validus, strong or healthy, the root behind invalid in both of its senses. Granting that a feeling is reasonable narrows an older logical meaning down to something warmer.
words.origin: Middle French valide, from Latin validus
hints: Latin for strong or healthy.
Logic used it long before feelings did.
words.connection: Approval offered to a feeling rather than a performance.

title: Too Online
blurb: Five words for the condition, and for the cure.

words.definition: Gone wild after a stretch of confinement.
words.note: From Latin fera, a wild animal. It described escaped livestock reverting to the wild long before it described anybody's behaviour after a week indoors.
words.origin: Middle French féral, from Late Latin ferālis
words.example: A pack of feral dogs.
hints: Latin for a wild animal.
First used of livestock that escaped.
words.connection: What a person becomes without daylight or company.

words.definition: Reads everything and posts nothing.
words.note: Probably from Middle English lurken, to lie hidden. Early message boards in the 1980s adopted it almost unchanged, and the meaning has not moved since.
hints: Message boards borrowed this one in the 1980s.
Lying hidden, in Middle English.
words.connection: Presence without participation, the default state of being online.

words.definition: The ground cover you are repeatedly told to go outside and touch.
words.note: From Old English graes, related to green and to grow. All three descend from a root meaning to sprout.
hints: Related to both green and grow.
What the famous instruction tells you to touch.
words.connection: The prescribed cure, named in the instruction itself.

words.definition: The organ said to rot from too much scrolling.
words.note: From Old English braegen. The complaint is older than the internet: brain-rot appears in Thoreau's Walden in 1854, grumbling that nobody worried about it the way they worried about potato rot.
hints: Thoreau complained about this one rotting in 1854.
The organ blamed for the whole condition.
words.connection: The part reportedly damaged by all of it.

words.definition: A single sitting in which far too much is consumed.
words.note: An English dialect word meaning to soak a wooden vessel until it stops leaking. It moved from soaking wood to soaking oneself, and then to episodes of television.
hints: Dialect for soaking a barrel watertight.
Television borrowed it from drinking.
words.connection: How the hours disappear once you have stopped noticing.

title: In the Lobby
blurb: Five words a generation learned from a loading screen.

words.definition: A strong player on a new account, beating beginners.
words.note: From Warcraft II, where two well-known players made fresh accounts under the names PapaSmurf and Smurfette so that opponents would agree to play them. The name stuck to the practice.
hints: Two players picked cartoon names to stay anonymous.
Strength disguised as inexperience.
words.connection: Hiding your skill behind a new name, which only a game lets you do.

words.definition: To win a team game almost single-handed.
words.note: From Old North French carier, to transport in a vehicle, the same root as car and cargo. The team sense is a short step from bearing a weight nobody else will.
hints: Shares a root with car and cargo.
Bearing a weight the rest of the team will not.
words.connection: Bearing four other people to a victory they did not earn.

words.definition: Weakens something that had become too strong.
words.note: Named after the brand of foam toys, on the logic that the weapon has been swapped for a harmless version. Its opposite, to buff, was borrowed from polishing instead.
hints: A foam toy brand gave this its name.
The opposite was borrowed from polishing.
words.connection: The correction applied when one option stops being a choice.

words.definition: To appear at a starting point.
words.note: From Anglo-French espaundre, to shed roe. Fish producing offspring in great numbers gave the word its sense of sudden mass appearance, which games then took literally.
hints: Fish and their roe gave us this word.
Sudden appearance, taken literally.
words.connection: Arriving from nowhere, which only happens somewhere like this.

words.definition: The room where everyone waits before it begins.
words.note: From medieval Latin lobia, a covered walkway, the same root as lodge. The political sense came from people waiting in the corridors of Parliament to catch members on their way past.
hints: Parliament's corridors gave politics a verb.
A covered walkway, in medieval Latin.
words.connection: The waiting room everything else happens after.

title: Modern Courtship
blurb: Five stages of meeting someone through a telephone.

words.definition: To move a finger across a screen and decide.
words.note: Originally a sweeping blow, probably related to sweep. It picked up the sense of theft, then of running a card through a reader, and finally the gesture itself.
hints: Probably related to sweep.
Meant theft before it meant a gesture.
words.connection: The gesture the whole arrangement is named after.

words.definition: Two people who both said yes.
words.note: From Old English gemaecca, a companion or mate. The fire-lighting kind is an entirely different word, from Old French mesche, a lamp wick.
words.origin: Old French mesche, from Vulgar Latin micca
words.example: He struck a match and lit his pipe.
hints: Old English for a companion or mate.
The fire-lighting kind is a different word entirely.
words.connection: The moment the arrangement decides you are both interested.

words.definition: Light exchanges that go nowhere in particular.
words.note: A shortening of chatter, which is imitative: the word was built to sound like the noise it describes.
hints: The longer form was built to sound like noise.
Exchanges that rarely arrive anywhere.
words.connection: What fills the week between agreeing and never meeting.

words.definition: Someone who cancels, and keeps cancelling.
words.note: From the sense of a thin loose piece that falls away. Calling an unreliable person one is American slang from the 1950s, carrying the same image of something that will not hold together.
words.origin: Old English flacca, from Old Norse flak
hints: American slang from the 1950s.
The image is of something not holding together.
words.connection: The outcome most of it arrives at.

words.definition: The small trace of interest that either catches or does not.
words.note: From Old English spearca. Using it for a trace of feeling is old: a spark of pity appears in English centuries before anyone used it about a first date.
words.example: A spark of interest.
hints: Old English, and older than romance.
A trace of fire standing in for feeling.
words.connection: The thing everyone claims to be looking for.

title: Mild Distress
blurb: Five states that stop well short of an actual crisis.

words.definition: Badly rattled by something small.
words.note: The standard past participle is shaken; this older form survived in dialect and in Black American English, which is where the emotional use comes from.
hints: An older past tense that never quite died.
Rattled rather than genuinely harmed.
words.connection: Rattled, but recoverable by the evening.

words.definition: Bitter about losing, and not hiding it.
words.note: Naval slang for a sailor long enough at sea to be weathered and short-tempered. The sense of sour resentment came ashore from there.
hints: Sailors were described this way first.
A taste standing in for resentment.
words.connection: Resentment that everyone can see and nobody will mention.

words.definition: More than the occasion called for.
words.note: A shortening of the Latin phrase extra ordinem, outside the usual order, which also gives extraordinary. The criticism is precise: someone is doing more than the moment ordered.
words.example: Found some extra change lying on the dresser.
hints: Latin for outside the usual order.
The complaint is about scale, not sincerity.
words.connection: Distress performed slightly larger than it is felt.

words.definition: Predictable in taste, and perfectly happy about it.
words.note: From base, the bottom of a thing, via Latin basis, a step or pedestal. The dismissive use is recent; for centuries the word meant fundamental, which was a compliment.
hints: Latin for a step or pedestal.
It was a compliment for several centuries.
words.connection: An insult only because taste became something to defend.

words.definition: Given to sudden changes of temper.
words.note: From Old English mod, which meant mind, spirit or courage rather than a passing humour. Someone described this way once meant a brave or proud one.
hints: Old English used its root for courage.
Once described the proud, not the sullen.
words.connection: Temper treated as weather rather than as a decision.

title: Laying the Table
blurb: Five things that turn dinner into an occasion.

words.definition: A flat dish used for serving or eating food.
words.note: Plate has meant a thin sheet of metal as well as dinnerware. That older sense survives in terms such as armour plate and licence plate.
words.origin: Old French plate, from Ancient Greek πλατύς
words.example: I filled my plate from the bountiful table.
hints: Often waits at every seat before a meal.
It gives a serving its own small territory.
words.connection: A plate is placed for each person at a prepared table.

words.definition: A hard transparent material, or a vessel made from it.
words.note: The material can be made by cooling molten sand so quickly that its particles never form a regular crystal pattern. English uses the same word for the material and for a drinking vessel.
hints: It can be clear, coloured, or carefully polished.
Water may be poured into one beside a meal.
words.connection: A glass is a common place setting for a drink.

words.definition: A tool or utensil with a sharp blade.
words.note: The silent initial letter records the word’s Norse ancestry. In older English it was pronounced, as it still is in related Scandinavian languages.
words.origin: Old English cnīf, from Old Norse knífr
words.example: He was looking for a knife to chop some steak.
hints: It has uses in a workshop as well as a kitchen.
At dinner it is usually paired with a fork.
words.connection: A knife is one of the utensils laid beside a plate.

words.definition: Woven or knitted fabric.
words.note: The word is related to Old English forms for a covering. Its use in tablecloth keeps that older sense close to the surface.
words.example: Woven cloth originated in Mesopotamia around 5000 BC.
hints: It begins as threads worked together.
It can cover a dining surface before anything is served.
words.connection: A cloth can cover and protect a dining table.

words.definition: A utensil with a small bowl on a handle.
words.note: Spoon comes from an Old English word for a chip of wood, probably because early examples resembled a splinter or shaving.
hints: It carries something without needing to pierce it.
Soup makes its purpose especially clear.
words.connection: A spoon completes a familiar set of table utensils.

title: Working With Wood
blurb: The material answers back in five different ways.

words.definition: The direction and visible pattern of fibres in wood.
words.note: Grain also names seeds and a tiny unit of weight. The shared idea is a small repeated structure that gives a material its character.
words.origin: Old French grain, from Latin grānum
words.example: Saw the board across the grain.
hints: It can run straight, curl, or catch the light.
A craftsperson usually follows it rather than fighting it.
words.connection: Grain is the natural pattern a woodworker reads in timber.

words.definition: A tool that shaves thin layers from wood to make it smooth.
words.note: The tool takes its name from the flat surface it creates. A hand plane can leave long curled shavings that show exactly what it has removed.
words.origin: Anglo-Norman plaine, from Late Latin plāna
hints: It removes less than a saw but more than sandpaper.
Its job is to make a board even and smooth.
words.connection: A plane shapes and flattens a piece of wood.

words.definition: A place where two pieces are joined together.
words.note: In furniture, a well-made joint can be stronger than a fastener alone. The same word is used for the meeting of bones in a body.
words.example: This rod is free to swing at the joint with the platform.
hints: It is a meeting point rather than a separate object.
A dovetail is a celebrated kind of this.
words.connection: A joint is where parts of a wooden object are fitted together.

words.definition: To cut a shape or pattern from a solid material.
words.note: Carve can describe both making a sculpture and dividing a roast. In both cases, a larger whole is deliberately cut into a useful form.
hints: It changes a solid piece by removing parts of it.
A sharp edge can turn timber into a figure or ornament.
words.connection: To carve is to shape wood by cutting material away.

words.definition: A coloured substance that changes the surface of a material.
words.note: Wood stain colours while leaving the grain visible, unlike an opaque paint. The word’s figurative sense of a mark on a reputation came later.
hints: It changes colour without necessarily hiding texture.
A finish may use it before a protective coat.
words.connection: A stain is used to colour and finish wooden surfaces.

title: Finding the Way
blurb: A journey viewed from the map rather than the window.

words.definition: A map or diagram that presents information clearly.
words.note: A nautical chart is built for navigation and includes dangers, depths and aids to steering. The word later widened to include graphs of any kind.
words.origin: Middle French charte, from Ancient Greek χάρτης
hints: It makes a large area legible at a glance.
Sailors consult one before moving through unfamiliar water.
words.connection: A chart helps a traveller understand where to go.
