words.definition: A way or course taken from one place to another.
words.note: Route entered English from French, and its pronunciation still varies by region. It can describe a bus line, a delivery run or a planned journey.
words.origin: Old French route, from Latin rupta [via]
words.example: The route was used so much that it formed a rut.
hints: It joins a departure to an arrival.
A detour asks you to change this.
words.connection: A route is the planned course of a journey.

words.definition: A path made or used by people or animals.
words.note: Trail began as a word for dragging something behind, which explains both a woodland path and the line left by a moving object.
words.origin: Old French trailler, from Latin tragula
words.example: The trail has gone cold.
hints: It may be worn into the ground over time.
Hikers follow one through country without roads.
words.connection: A trail is a route made by repeated passage.

words.definition: A person or thing that shows the way.
words.note: Guide works as a noun and a verb. A guidebook can lead someone without ever travelling alongside them.
words.origin: Old French guide, from Old Occitan guida
hints: It can be a person, a book, or a helpful sign.
Its value is clearest in an unfamiliar place.
words.connection: A guide helps a traveller choose the right way.

words.definition: The direction toward the North Pole.
words.note: On most modern maps this direction sits at the top, a convention rather than a universal law. A compass needle is used to find it.
words.example: Minnesota is in the north of the USA.
hints: Most maps place it above the other directions.
A compass points toward this end of the world.
words.connection: North is a cardinal direction used for navigation.

title: After the Match
blurb: Five small things that make competition matter.

words.definition: The number of points earned in a game or contest.
words.note: Score also means a group of twenty, a written piece of music, and a mark cut into a surface. The sporting sense is another kind of record.
words.origin: Old English scoru, from Old Norse skor
words.example: The player with the highest score is the winner.
hints: It changes when a side succeeds.
A board may display it above the field.
words.connection: A score records what each side has achieved in a match.

words.definition: A small metal award given for achievement.
words.note: Medals have marked service, learning and athletic success for centuries. The familiar gold, silver and bronze sequence became standard in modern international sport.
words.origin: Middle French medaille, from Classical Latin medius
hints: It is small enough to hang from a ribbon.
Podium finishers may receive one.
words.connection: A medal recognises an outstanding result in competition.

words.definition: Something given or won in recognition of success.
words.note: Prize is related to price, but its meaning shifted from value paid to a thing worth winning. It can be tangible or simply an honour.
words.origin: Old French prise, from Latin prēndere
hints: It may be offered before an event begins.
Winning can bring this even without money.
words.connection: A prize is awarded to reward a successful competitor.

words.definition: A shout or expression of encouragement and approval.
words.note: Cheer once meant the face or expression, then a mood, before becoming a sound of support. Its older sense survives in the phrase good cheer.
words.origin: Anglo-Norman chere, from Old French chiere; in English since the 18th century
hints: It can rise suddenly from a crowd.
Supporters make this when a side does well.
words.connection: A cheer is the sound spectators make to support a team.

words.definition: Objectives to be achieved, or points scored in certain sports.
words.note: The sporting and personal senses share the same image: a defined end point to work toward. In football, the word can name both the target structure and the point scored there.
hints: They can be scored, set, or revised.
A team pursues these on a field while a person sets them for a year.
words.connection: Goals give a sporting contest both its target and its result.

title: Things We Keep
blurb: Small objects that are asked to hold more than themselves.

words.definition: A photograph, especially a printed or digital image.
words.note: Photo is a shortening of photograph, built from Greek roots meaning light and writing. It records an image by using light to make a lasting trace.
hints: It preserves an instant after it has passed.
An album can hold many of these.
words.connection: A photo can keep a visible record of a memory.

words.definition: A book in which someone records daily events or thoughts.
words.note: Diary comes from the Latin word for day. It began as a daily record of events before becoming a private personal habit.
words.example: They kept separate diaries. His was on paper and her diary was on her computer's hard drive.
hints: Its entries are usually dated.
It can keep thoughts that were not meant for an audience.
words.connection: A diary keeps a personal record over time.

words.definition: A small object that stands for an idea, feeling or right.
words.note: A token may be a souvenir, a voucher or a symbolic gesture. What matters is the meaning it carries beyond its material value.
words.example: Everyone pick a token (hat, wheelbarrow, thimble, etc.) and place it on the Start square.
hints: Its value often comes from what it represents.
A small souvenir can become one.
words.connection: A token is kept because it stands for something larger.

words.definition: A flat surface fixed to a wall or furniture for holding things.
words.note: Shelf is related to the nautical word shelf, once used for a sandbank or ledge. Both senses describe a horizontal support or projection.
words.example: We keep the old newspapers on the bottom shelf of the cupboard, and our photos on the top shelf.
hints: It turns a wall into storage.
Books, framed pictures and souvenirs may gather here.
words.connection: A shelf gives saved objects a place to remain visible.

words.definition: A small printed label used to show payment for post.
words.note: Stamps also leave an impression when pressed into ink, metal or wax. Postal ones became collectable because each carries a small design and a date in history.
hints: It is small enough to collect in an album.
A letter may need one before it can travel.
words.connection: A stamp can be kept as a small record of place and time.

title: On the Stage
blurb: The work that exists for an audience in the dark.

words.definition: A raised area where performers appear before an audience.
words.note: Stage once referred to a stopping place on a journey. Its theatrical sense grew from temporary platforms erected for public performances.
words.origin: Old French estage, from Old French ester
hints: It is empty until someone steps into view.
Curtains and spotlights often frame it.
words.connection: A stage is the physical place where a performance is presented.

words.definition: Parts played by performers, or functions people take on.
words.note: Role came into English through French from a word for a roll of paper. A performer’s part was once written on such a roll.
hints: A cast divides these among its members.
Outside theatre, a person may have several at work and home.
words.connection: Roles are the parts performers take in a production.

words.definition: A section of a play, film or story set in one place or time.
words.note: Scene comes from a Greek word for a stage building. It can now mean a dramatic episode, a view, or a public commotion.
words.origin: Middle French scene, from Ancient Greek σκηνή
hints: It changes when the action moves somewhere else.
A script is commonly divided into acts and these.
words.connection: A scene is a distinct unit in a staged story.

words.definition: A story written or performed for the stage or screen.
words.note: The word comes from Greek for an action or deed. Its everyday use for exaggerated conflict keeps that sense of action alive.
words.origin: Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα
words.example: The author released her latest drama, which became a best-seller.
hints: It may be written, rehearsed and performed.
Conflict gives this form its movement.
words.connection: Drama is the story form performers bring to an audience.

words.definition: Objects used by performers during a production.
words.note: Props is a shortening of properties, the theatrical term for objects owned or used by a company. A letter, a cup or a sword can all serve this function.
hints: They are handled during a performance.
A convincing room on stage may be full of these.
words.connection: Props are the objects that help performers make a scene believable.

title: In the Garden
blurb: Five signs that something patient is growing.

words.definition: A living thing that usually grows in soil and makes energy from light.
words.note: Plant is also a verb for putting something in the ground and a noun for a factory. The living sense remains the centre of the word’s everyday use.
words.origin: Old English plante, from Latin planta
hints: It needs light, water and time.
Its leaves make energy from sunlight.
words.connection: A plant is the living subject of a garden.

words.definition: Soil, ground, or the planet on which people live.
words.note: Earth has kept both its local and cosmic senses for centuries. In a garden it means the material that holds roots, water and nutrients.
hints: It can be held in a hand or seen from space.
Roots push down into this as they grow.
words.connection: Earth is the soil from which a garden grows.

words.definition: A flower, or the act of producing flowers.
words.note: Bloom is related to blossom, though modern English tends to use it for a flower’s best moment. It can also describe a healthy flush of colour in a face.
words.example: You will stop all bloom if you let the flowers go to seed.
hints: It is a brief bright stage in a plant’s year.
A rose opens into one.
words.connection: A bloom is the flowering result of garden work.

words.definition: The parts of a plant that anchor it and take in water.
words.note: Roots are usually hidden, which makes them a useful metaphor for origins and deep connections. They can spread far beyond the visible stem.
words.example: The centipede twisted and turned through the maze of roots.
hints: They work below the surface.
They hold a plant in place and draw up water.
words.connection: Roots anchor a garden plant and feed it from below.

words.definition: Plants growing where they are not wanted.
words.note: Weed is a judgment rather than a botanical category. The same plant can be welcomed for its flowers in one place and removed from another.
hints: Its identity depends on where it chooses to grow.
Gardeners pull these from places reserved for other plants.
words.connection: Weeds are plants competing with a gardener’s intended growth.

title: At the Desk
blurb: The quiet equipment behind a finished page.

words.definition: A thin material made for writing, printing or wrapping.
words.note: Paper was developed in ancient China from fibres suspended in water and pressed into sheets. It eventually displaced parchment for most everyday writing.
words.origin: Anglo-Norman paper, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος
words.example: Draw on the paper! Not on the walls!
hints: It begins as fibres and ends as a thin surface.
Words, drawings and receipts are often kept on it.
words.connection: Paper is the surface on which desk work is recorded.

words.definition: Short written records made to remember information.
words.note: Note came through Latin from a word for a mark or sign. It can also refer to a musical sound, preserving the idea of a small meaningful mark.
hints: They are brief enough to capture before a thought escapes.
A meeting may end with a page full of these.
words.connection: Notes preserve the small pieces of work done at a desk.

words.definition: Bound collections of written or printed pages.
words.note: Book is related to an old Germanic word for beech, perhaps because early writing was sometimes scratched onto beechwood tablets.
hints: They contain more than one page and one sitting.
A shelf is built to keep these upright.
words.connection: Books are the longer works consulted and kept near a desk.

words.definition: To form letters or words in order to communicate.
words.note: Write comes from an Old English word for scratching or drawing. The physical mark came first; its use for language followed naturally.
words.example: Your son has been writing on the wall.
hints: It turns a thought into marks another person can read.
A blank page asks you to do this.
words.connection: To write is the central action a desk is made to support.

words.definition: The name of a book, work, office or position.
words.note: Title comes from a Latin word for an inscription or label. It still sits at the threshold of a work, telling a reader how to approach it.
words.origin: Old English titul, from Latin titulus
words.example: He looked for books with the word `jazz' in the title.
hints: It appears before the first chapter begins.
A book’s cover usually carries one.
words.connection: A title labels the work produced or consulted at a desk.
